History lesson: Last time the contenders met in a final
A whole new competition starts this weekend as eight contenders go into battle across four matches in three days with one goal in mind.
The Panthers have proven themselves the masters of finals football across the past five years while the Roosters (2002, 2013, 2018, 2019), Sharks (2016), Cowboys (2015), Rabbitohs (2014) and Knights (2001) all have premierships to their name in the NRL era.
The Dolphins are in their first ever finals series and their opponents the Warriors have been here 10 times but never come away with a title.
With two sudden-death showdowns and two qualifying finals coming up this weekend, NRL.com takes a look at the most recent September clash between the sides.
Knights v Rabbitohs
2020 elimination final
The Rabbitohs and Knights have only met once in finals football, and it came in exactly the same circumstances as Friday night at Allianz Stadium.
Six years ago, South Sydney and Newcastle finished sixth and seventh respectively before meeting in a sudden-death elimination final.
Now, with the Rabbitohs sixth and the Knights seventh again, history is repeating itself as the two sides prepare to do battle for a place in the semi-finals.
There is still plenty of familiar faces from that 2020 clash.
Match Highlights: Rabbitohs v Knights
Alex Johnston, Campbell Graham, Cody Walker, Tevita Tatola and Cameron Murray were all part of the Rabbitohs side that night six years ago, while Dane Gagai, who will now wear a Knights jersey, also featured for South Sydney.
Newcastle has just three players remaining from that team in Kalyn Ponga, Bradman Best and Jacob Saifiti.
And if Friday night follows the script from 2020, South Sydney will be hoping for a repeat of the result.
The Rabbitohs blew the Knights away 46-20, with Johnston crossing twice alongside Tatola, two names who will again feature in the elimination final six years later.
Alex Johnston finds the line during the Bunnies' 46-20 win over the Knights in the 2020 elimination final.
Roosters v Panthers
2024 qualifying final
The Roosters and Panthers know each other all too well when it comes to September football.
Their last three finals meetings have all come in the qualifying final, and once again, they find themselves in exactly the same position.
Their most recent showdown came in 2024, when Penrith began its march towards a fourth straight premiership with a commanding 30-10 victory over the Roosters at BlueBet Stadium.
Panthers v Roosters – Finals Week 1, 2024
There is still plenty of familiar faces from that clash, with the Panthers’ champion core and the Roosters’ star-studded spine preparing to renew one of the competition’s fiercest finals rivalries.
Penrith has won four of its past five finals meetings with the Roosters, but with a preliminary-final spot and a precious week off on the line, history will count for little when these two heavyweight clubs collide again.
Yep, he's back!
Sharks v Cowboys
2024 semi-final
The Sharks and Cowboys have plenty of finals history, and their most recent meeting could provide the perfect blueprint for another high-stakes showdown.
The two clubs have met six times in finals football, with the teams splitting those matches at three apiece but it was the Sharks who had the last laugh.
Sharks v Cowboys – Finals Week 2, 2024
When the sides met in the 2024 semi-final at Allianz Stadium, Cronulla held on for a 26-18 victory to book a place in the preliminary final and end the Cowboys’ campaign.
Braydon Trindall played a starring role that night, scoring twice, and now, two years on, he’ll return from injury with another chance to make his mark.
This time, there is no second chance.
With both sides fighting to keep their premiership dreams alive, Saturday afternoon’s clash promises another chapter in a finals rivalry that has produced plenty of drama over the years.

'No one gave us a chance': Chasing pack desperate to defy history
Cronulla captain Blayke Brailey will draw on NSW's unexpected State of Origin series victory as the Sharks look to defy history by becoming the first team in more than three decades to win the NRL premiership from outside the top four.
It's been 31 years since Terry Lamb led the Bulldogs from sixth place to premiership glory in 1995. While plenty of clubs have come close, the challenge of winning four-straight sudden death finals has proved an insurmountable task.
It's a stat this year's contenders are determined to change, with the Sharks leading a group of teams desperate to rewrite the record books.
Brailey made his NSW debut during this year's series and returned from a broken arm to help the Blues defy history when they upset the Maroons in a Suncorp Stadium decider.
Few gave Laurie Daley's men a chance when they travelled north for Game Three and Brailey said Cronulla will adopt a similar mindset throughout the finals campaign.
"We have the underdog mentality and we all enjoy that approach," Brailey told NRL.com. "No one gives us a chance but it's similar to the Origin series in Game Three when no one gave us a chance. We found it a way and we turned it around.
"People thought we'd just turn up and lose and I'm sure in this finals series people just expect the same. We know what it takes now to deal with that pressure. We've got a few players in our side that love the underdog mentality so we're taking it all in and excited for the weeks to come."
Trindall raring to return for Cowboys clash
Cronulla have received a major boost for Saturday's clash with North Queensland at Allianz Stadium with five-eighth Braydon Trindall named to return from a dislocated shoulder.
The Sharks are in a familiar position entering this year's finals series, Craig Fitzgibbon's men also finishing fifth last season before surging to the preliminary final.
The Cowboys don't have to look too far for inspiration in their bid for the premiership, with Jason Taumalolo and Coen Hess playing a key role in the club's charge from eighth to the 2017 grand final.
North Queensland have also received a major boost in recent weeks with star halfback Tom Dearden making a successful return from an ankle injury.
Also looking to defy history this year are the Rabbitohs and Knights, who will do battle in a Friday night blockbuster at Allianz Stadium to kick off the weekend.
Tom Dearden Try
Both teams also have a track record of deep finals runs from outside the top four, with Newcastle progressing to the preliminary final in 2013 after finishing seventh on the ladder.
Fullback Kalyn Ponga has returned to the form that saw him claim the Dally M Medal in 2023 and has the potential to emulate Reece Walsh's stunning run to the premiership with the Broncos last year.
South Sydney went from seventh to a prelim the last time they played finals football in 2022.
The Rabbitohs are peaking at the right time of year, with star centre Latrell Mitchell back on deck and powerful back-rower David Fifita back to his damaging best.
Latrell Mitchell returns for the Rabbitohs
With finals experience spread across the park, South Sydney captain Cameron Murray is confident his team has the talent to upstage their more fancied rivals.
"We're not paying too much attention to the history books," Murray said. "We're paying attention to the footy we can play and the product we can put on the field.
"If we're disciplined and we turn up with the right attitude, I'm confident we can be successful in the finals.
"We have a lot of big game experience in the team so that helps, but for us it's about our discipline and turning up to play the footy we know we can play."

'Falling into place': New mindset driving Latrell's premiership charge
South Sydney star Latrell Mitchell is ready to translate off-field stability into premiership success as he prepares to end a four-year wait to play finals football.
Mitchell will take centre-stage on Friday night when he plays his first finals game since the 2022 preliminary final as the Rabbitohs host Newcastle in a sudden-death showdown.
It's been an eventful four years for the South Sydney star, who has battled a string of injuries on the field at the same time he has become increasingly comfortable with his status as an Indigenous leader.
Latrell Mitchell returns for the Rabbitohs
Mitchell's maturity was on display this week when he fronted the media in the lead up to Friday's elimination final and reflected on the challenges he's faced throughout his career.
"My advice to any young fella coming through is that adversity is always going to be there and challenges are always going to be faced," Mitchell said. "It's just the way you come out of it [that matters].
"The moments I've had in my time and my career and what I've learned, they're just lessons, they're not losses. For me moving forward, I've lived probably a lot more experiences than most older men, so for me, it is what it is.
"I love what I'm doing, I love the team, and everything's just falling into place. I'm just cruising along now and I just want to play footy and have fun."

It's hard to believe it's been a decade since Mitchell made his NRL debut as a fresh-faced 18-year-old for the Roosters in 2016.
It quickly became clear the youngster was destined for superstardom and it didn't take long for Mitchell to deliver on his potential.
A NSW debut came in 2018, with his first Kangaroos jumper coming later that season and he helped set up the winning try in the 2019 grand final to secure his second NRL premiership.
Tedesco finishes blindside raid by Roosters
It hasn't all been smooth sailing, however. Mitchell has long been one of the most polarising figures in the game and was not afraid to speak his mind earlier in his career.
His outspoken personality drew criticism from some fans, prompting the centre to step out of the spotlight in the past few years.
A country boy from the NSW mid-north coast, Mitchell has found peace on his farm in Taree where he hopes to one day raise his four children.
"Coming from a small town, Taree, footy was everything," Mitchell said. "It was the only way I got out of town and created a dream and everything that I wanted to achieve.
"For me, it's just going back to that and never forgetting that young fella who was running around with his brothers, fighting around, carrying on, and having a laugh. That's what it was about back then, and I just want to carry that on to the big stage, keep that feel, and just be there for your mates and help them out."
While the farm is Mitchell's happy place, he's just as confident taking centre-stage under the bright lights of a rugby league field.
In many ways it's the place the centre is most comfortable. The bigger the stage, the better Mitchell performs.

Rabbitohs v Knights: Tallis gets green light; Manuleleua's miracle
The Rabbitohs are back in the finals for the first time since 2022 and riding high after a big win over the Roosters and the emotion of Jai Arrow's 100th game celebrations.
With Latrell Mitchell getting through a full 80 minutes against the Roosters and looking in ominous form, the Bunnies are primed for a huge performance in front of their home fans.
After sitting fourth with eight rounds to play, the Knights won just three of their final eight games to finish seventh as injuries and suspension took a toll.
The Knights have done a remarkable job to turn their fortunes around and finishing last in 2025 and they will be banking on the brilliance of Kalyn Ponga, Bradman Best and Fletcher Sharpe to keep the dream alive for another week.
The two meetings between these sides during the regular season produced a total of 130 points with the Knights getting home 42-38 in Round 9 before the Rabbitohs turned the tables 26-24 in Round 19.
A tighter contest can be expected in the pressure cooker atmosphere of a sudden-death final but there's enough attacking weapons on both sides to ensure an entertaining night for fans at Allianz Stadium.

NRL Casualty Ward: Pec pain over for Ford; Crichton good to go
The Warriors have received a huge boost ahead of their qualifying final against the Dolphins with gun forward Jackson Ford set to return from a pectoral injury.
After making a dynamic start to the season in which he averaged 161 run metres and 41 tackles per game, Ford suffered the injury in Round 16 against the Cowboys and initial fears were he could miss the rest of the year.
Ford has been named on the bench for the blockbuster Go Media Stadium showdown against the Dolphins, who get Selwyn Cobbo (ankle), back-rower Kulikefu Finefeuiaki (knee) and five-eighth Kodi Nikorima (hamstring) back for their first ever final.
Nikorima and Finefeuiaki were given last week off to get over niggling injuries ahead of the finals.
The Roosters also have a star forward returning for their qualifying final against Penrith with Angus Crichton back after 11 games out with a foot injury.
Also back on deck at the Roosters are Victor Radley (concussion) and a posse of stars who were rested in Round 27 including James Tedesco , Daly Cherry-Evans and Rob Toia .
The Rabbitohs have Tallis Duncan back from a hamstring injury but will be without veteran back-rower Euan Aitken for the rest of the season after he fractured his scapula in the win over the Roosters.
The injury is a cruel blow for 31-year-old Aitken, who was on the verge of playing in just the second finals match of his 223-game career.
Aitken's only finals appearance came with the Dragons in his debut season in 2015.

Cowboys trio Zac Laybutt (concussion), Griffin Neame (toe) and Jeremiah Nanai (knee) all return after missing the loss to Canberra in Round 27 but Murray Taulagi remains sidelined with ongoing concussion issues.
Storm winger Siulagi Tuimalatu-Brown was taken to hospital as a precaution after he was stretchered from Ocean Protect Stadium last Saturday night.
The game was just five minutes old when Tuimalatu-Brown was taken low by Cam McInnes and Michael Gabrael over the top, with the Sharks debutant making high contact.
In an update on Sunday morning , the Storm said initial assessments indicate the youngster does not have a severe spinal injury but he will undergo further testing due to numbness in his arm.
"Siulagi was admitted to hospital overnight after concerns for a neck injury," the statement said. "There was no severe spinal injury on initial assessment but he will undergo further scans today due to concerns for some ongoing numbness to the arm."
The Storm also lost halfback Jahrome Hughes to a hamstring injury late in the first half after he was twisted awkwardly while trying to clean up a loose ball.
Hughes will be sent for scans and faces a nervous wait for the results with the Kiwis' World Cup opener just six weeks away.

How Adam and Millie turned the Book of Feuds into a romance novel
It seems the love of a Rooster has helped this South Sydney Rabbitoh get back on the field in time to help his club try to win a 22nd NRL premiership.
And who said Roosters and Rabbitohs hate each other? Have you met the Elliotts?
Clearly Adam and Millie Elliott have no problem washing their jerseys and training gear together.
“It probably doesn’t get touched by us because there’s no Rabbitohs NRLW side, so there’s a bit of a loophole there at the moment,” Adam told NRL.com.
“If I’m at a game cheering for the Roosters NRLW side if they were paying Souths that would turn a few people off.
“But we’ve both jumped around in our careers a fair bit.
You’re kidding yourself if you’re not loyal to your wife or husband in whatever team they play for
Millie is heading for another finals campaign herself with the Roosters NRLW side completing an unbeaten season to secure the club's third minor premiership.
Alongside Hall of Fame prop Glenn Lazarus, Millie is the only other player to win premierships with three different clubs - Lazarus with the Raiders, Broncos and Storm, Elliott with the Broncos, Knights and Roosters.
In fact, it’s Millie’s support that Adam credits as one of the defining factors in him getting back on the field earlier than expected after a shocking ankle injury in Round 12 and then an adductor muscle strain in his groin in Round 24. He had already missed the opening nine round of the season with a torn calf.
Adam Elliott penalty Try
“I like the fact I can heal quick because it means people aren’t telling me I’m too old,” he said.
“I think being hard-headed, especially with the ankle. That was a big one coming back from that but I set myself a goal and got there.
“Obviously it helps a lot having Millie at home because she knows exactly what it takes for a footy player to play each week.
“So our smooth home life makes it easier for me to focus on my rehab. She gives me so much support in helping me get back and she’s a playing herself.
“It’s broken her heart as it’s broken mine with the injuries I’ve had the last couple of years. She’s been massive.”
Elliott is on the bench for Friday night’s elimination final against his old club, the Knights.
This will be his fourth finals series with his third different club – Raiders in 2022, Knights in 2023-24.
Inside Camp: Millie Elliott
Since making his NRL debut in 2016 with the Bulldogs, Elliott has picked up a few new tricks in the rehab department that weren’t available back then.
“Things like red-light therapy, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, which all help me to prepare my muscles for training sessions and games," he said.
“It’s just the combination of all that – diving in and doing those things that I know help my recovery and that includes the usuals like bone broth, collagen and getting lots of good sleep.”

The South Sydney Rabbitohs will head into the finals as heavy favourites to advance out of the first week when they clash with the understrength Newcastle Knights on Friday evening.
For the second year in a row, the minor premiers don't open the finals, but that gives us an immediate knockout fixture.
The Rabbitohs have been one of the more inconsistent teams throughout the course of the year, but their ability to put points up in a hurry and dominate on the back of it, has seen then finish in sixth spot, and earn the all-important hosting rights this weekend.
In truth, that is as big a boost as any, with the road trip to the Hunter being a tough one at the best of times.
Their recent form has continued those inconsistency question marks.
A big win over the resting Roosters, a big win over the Titans, and wins over the Eels and Bulldogs litter their final five weeks of the season, but that is all offset by a 19-point loss to the New Zealand Warriors where they conceded 45 in Round 25 on home soil.
Maybe that isn't the end of the world if it's a one-off, but defensive issues are certainly the key question mark for the Rabbitohs.
The Rabbitohs have only conceded more than 40 points twice this season, but they have conceded more than 30 on nine occasions.
Maybe, if there is a positive to be taken, it's that the bulk of those were in the first half of the season, and they seem to have slowly adjusted to the rules and pace of the game throughout the course of the year.
They are still heavily reliant on a number of players to spark their attack, led by Latrell Mitchell , while selection questions also linger heading into the finals with Matt Dufty recalled at fullback.
At the very least, South Sydney aren't all that understrength as they head in to the business stage of the year.
The same can't be said for the Knights, who have been, in a word brave.
Twin season ending injuries to Dylan Brown and Dylan Lucas in Round 21 against the Sydney Roosters had the potential to nuke their season on the spot, but instead, they have kept fighting.
Wins against the Broncos, Raiders and Titans all but locked up their finals spot, although the concern for Newcastle is they copped 44 points against Manly and 46 against the Warriors leading in to their bye that concluded the regular season.
That game against the Warriors was played with 12 men for the most part after Jacob Saifiti ended his season with a horror high tackle.
That is three big names out for Justin Holbrook's side, and while they have outperformed expectations, it's tough to see how so much experience off the park come the biggest time of year allows them to put up a winning performance.
That all said, prior to their final two games of the year, the Knights have had only conceded more than 40 points once all year, way back in Round 6 against the Wests Tigers , and it has been clear for the most part that the playing group have bought in to everything Justin Holbrook has asked for.

Phoenix rises as Holbrook looks to keep the dream alive
Justin Holbrook doesn’t want the dream year to end.
In his first season at the helm, Holbrook has transformed the Knights from wooden spooners into a finals contender, and with an elimination final against Souths looming on Friday night, he is adamant his side can keep their remarkable revival alive.
Newcastle finished seventh after winning 14 of their 24 games, earning their first finals appearance since 2023 after a season that has tested the depth and resilience of their squad.
Marquee signing Dylan Brown suffered an ACL injury in Round 21 while Dylan Lucas (ankle), Jacob Saifiti (suspended) and Trey Mooney (shoulder) are also gone for the season.
Skipper Kalyn Ponga has played just 15 matches and centre Bradman Best 14 but still the Knights hung tough to finish seventh.
“It’s a reward for being consistent during the year,” Holbrook said.
“We don’t want to be just happy to be there. We want to be winning games.
Tyson Frizell celebrates game 300
“I loved this year and I want it to continue.”
That belief has been there since Holbrook took charge of pre-season training last November.
The Knights entered 2026 determined to put last year’s wooden spoon behind them, but the prospect of September football was never seen as an unrealistic target with the addition of star playmaker Brown.
“Since November we were confident once we started pre-season training,” Holbrook said.
“When you think about finals and the teams that are in it versus the teams that aren’t in it, everyone should pat themselves on the back. It is hard to get into.”
Bradman Best Try
Getting there, however, is only half the job.
The Knights now face a Rabbitohs side hitting its best form at the business end of the season, with the added motivation of doing it for their mate Jai Arrow.
Holbrook knows exactly where the danger lies.
“We have a big job to do,” he said.
“They are threats. They are playing this good right at the end of the season, so we need to do a job on their key guys.”
But there is no shortage of confidence in the Newcastle camp.
“I’m confident that if we play well, we will win,” Holbrook said.
And he has received the perfect boost at the perfect time.
Phoenix Crossland returns at hooker after undergoing keyhole knee surgery, with the 26-year-old coming back into the side after being crowned Newcastle’s player of the year with the Danny Buderus Medal.
Phoenix Crossland Try
“It’s great that he got to freshen up. He’s had a long, hard year for us, playing through a lot of pain and being uncomfortable in a lot of games,” Holbrook said.
“Phoenix has been terrific.
“We need him back and we’ve got him. We are a much better side with him in it.”

Two into seven won't go but Bud and Jamie find the solution
Two talented South Sydney players have been duelling for the Rabbitohs halfback jersey but both have such deep respect for the other that there will be no bunny fight over it.
Jamie Humphreys and Jayden Sullivan are both 24 and both joined the Rabbitohs in 2025.
They are now about to play in their first NRL finals series, when Souths play the Knights in a sudden-death semi-final at Allianz Stadium.
Humphreys had the inside running for the No.7 last season and up until Round 9 this year, when a rib injury put him on the sidelines for three weeks.
In came Ashton Ward and Humphreys became the everywhere-man for coach Wayne Bennett playing at lock, hooker and back row as well as the halves.
Ward suffered a season-ending hamstring tear in Round 23 and in came Sullivan for the final four games of the regular season.
Sullivan and Humphreys played in the halves for the last 13 minutes of the 50-20 over the Roosters in Round 27, when five-eighth Cody Walker was given an early mark.
Jamie Humphreys Try
They are both open about coveting the No.7 but are willing to work hard at training together and let the supercoach Wayne Bennett decide.
“All of us in the spine talk a lot and I was lucky enough to play a fair bit alongside Cody last year,” Humphreys told NRL.com.
“I’ve been pretty much on the same page as Cody and although I’ve not played as much with Jayden, I feel just as connected with him.”
Sullivan enjoys the friendly rivalry with Humphreys and wants him in his team regardless of who plays halfback.
“With Jamie he just puts the team first,” Sullivan said.
Jayden Sullivan Try
“Obviously he wants to play a certain position and I want that same position.
“But he’s a really good person and he’s going to have a wonderful career.
"He’s one of our best trainers – just look at his physique and you can see that.
“He’s a player that staff are always trying to get off the field after training because he wants to stay out there and do extras.”
Humphreys is looking at the upside of being called on to cover a number of positions off the bench.
“I think taking opportunities in different positions exposes me to different scenarios,” he said.
“If I bring that back to being a half, now that I’ve been defending in the middle a lot of this year, that’s going to help me a lot in the halves defensively.
“I definitely had to toughen up a bit to play in the middle. And I’m gladly taking all those lessons.
“Certainly elements of all that can only help me going forward when I get a chance back in the halves.”
Cody Walker finding space as usual
As for his relationship with Sullivan, he has seen the fight in him after coming from the Dragons and Wests Tigers with limited game time but still the hunger.
“He’s really putting his best foot forward and playing with a lot of confidence which is awesome to see after some of the ups and downs he’s had,” Humphreys said.
“We’re winning with him at No.7 so let’s hope he keeps that streak going.”
For his part, Walker has a connection with both players but admires what Humphreys is doing.
“I don’t many players that can come off the bench and play lock, hooker, half, five-eighth so Jamie's versatility is so valuable in our team and he’s got no issues with doing any of them," Walker said.
“There’s not many people in the NRL that can handle those types of roles.”

items.body_excerpt:
They can be my wingmen anytime: Ponga pins faith in flyers
The bye in the final round may well have denied Newcastle flyers Greg Marzhew and Dominic Young the chance to claim the crown as the NRL's best wingmen.
Heading into Round 27 and the Knights pair had 44 tries between them – 24 to Marzhew and 20 to Young.
Right on their tail were Penrith’s Tom Jenkins and Brian To’o with a combined tally of 42.
But while the Knights had their feet up during a bye, To’o scored the first of the Panthers' seven tries against Wests Tigers and Jenkins bagged a double giving them 45 for the season.
On Friday the Knights wingmen oppose another two prolific finishers in South Sydney’s Alex Johnston (30 tries) and Campbell Graham (13) in the elimination final at Allianz Stadium.
Knights skipper Kalyn Ponga is backing his dynamic duo to outscore the Rabbitohs and is staggered by the finishing power of Marzhew and Young.
Dom-inating display from Young
“It’s crazy. And that’s not just for the tries but the work they do out of our backfield,” Ponga told NRL.com.
“Some of the carries they take I’d hate to take but they just do it – charge head-on – without us asking them to do all that.
“I know they just love it because they know what an important part good wingers can play in a team.”
Adding another twist to tale is the fact Marzhew needs just one try to equal Young's club record for most tries in a season (25 in 2023).
Five-course meal: Marzhew feasts on Dragons
Having endured grand final defeats in the 2017 Holden Cup U20s decider with Parramatta and the 2019 NSW Cup grand final with Wentworthville Magpies, Marzhew would love nothing better than to stand on top of the podium come October 4.
Young was part of the England side that suffered a heartbreaking 27-26 loss to Samoa in the World Cup semi-final in 2022 and played in the Roosters side that was blown away by the Storm in a preliminary final in 2024.
Ponga said the pair had earned the respect of their teammates for their individual skills and would play a leading role in the club's push for a first premiership since 2001.
“They are both special in their own right,” he said.
Knights v Rabbitohs – Round 9, 2026
“Dom has incredible speed and then Greg has incredible strength. They are different body shapes but they have that same great anticipation.
“They’ve even got a little battle going on between them just to keep things nice and competitive – what is it about wingers trying to out-score each other?
“But they’ve put a lot of work in – both of them – it just doesn’t happen to be that solid in such small spaces at times down the touchline.”
Both players celebrated their 100-game milestones this year – Marzhew is now on 110 NRL games and Young 115 – but it's a premiership they crave and that quest begins at Allianz Stadium on Friday night.
